newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton rates seen down in India, up in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton rates seen down in India, up in Pakistan.

text.p: Cotton rates are likely to fall in India on higher crop arrivals and rise in Pakistan on lower estimates of the new harvest, dealers said on Thursday.
Traders said India's cash-strapped cotton trade was heading for a boom driven by a liberal credit policy and a bumper crop.
They said the lifting of credit controls on cotton by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) at the weekend was welcomed by traders, who had been facing a severe liquidity crunch.
"The RBI policy is timely. It will definitely help orderly marketing of cotton," an official of the East India Cotton Association said.
Traders in Bombay said cotton arrivals from the 1996/97 (October/September) crop had picked up this week, depressing the prices of Punjab varieties.
"Punjab cotton initially climbed after the RBI policy cheered market sentiment, but the rally lost steam following heavy new crop arrivals," said a trader.
In spot, Punjab saw-ginned fell 30-35 rupees to 1,625/1,700 rupees per maund (37.32 kg). Daily arrivals in Punjab rose to 16,000/18,000 170-kg bales from 8,000/10,000 bales a week ago.
Bengal-deshi (ready delivery) settled 30-50 rupees lower at 960/1,020 rupees per maund, but Gujarat varieties gained on reports of poor arrivals due to unseasonal rains.
In spot, Gujarat Kalyan rose by 100 rupees to 12,900/13,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and Gujarat Sankar-4 (long-staple) by 100 rupees to 20,600/21,300 rupees per candy.
"Prices may ease further in the next few days under the pressure of new crop arrivals," one broker said.
In Pakistan, cotton rates jumped this week following Tuesday's 7.86 percent devaluation of the rupee against the dollar and imposition of new taxes, dealers said.
Prices also rose on fears that the crop may reach only nine million 375-lb bales, against a targeted 10 million.
The crop, which growers first estimated at 10.5 million bales, was now expected to come in at 9.0 to 9.2 million bales owing to pest damage, one dealer said.
"The crop estimates are fluctuating up and down, hurting the trade," said one broker, who said a clearer picture might emerge after a growers meeting in Multan on November 3.
Exporters went to the sidelines after the devaluation. "Prices are not workable for exports," one exporter said.
Exporters had registered 9,665 bales for export with the state-run Export Promotion Bureau by October 22.
In the kerb market, NIAB-78 rose to 2,200 rupees per maund from 2,150, broker Nasim Usman at the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) said.
